letter.title: About this letter
paragraphs: Ephesians presents itself as a letter from Paul, written while he was a prisoner. If so, it most likely dates to about AD 60–62, when Paul was held in Rome, several years after he left the city. Either way, it was written after the events you walk through in this game.

Scholars are divided about who wrote it. Many hold that Paul wrote it himself. Many others think a follower of Paul wrote it in his name after Paul’s death, perhaps around AD 80–90. Careful readers stand on both sides, and this game does not try to settle the question. When the notes in this game say ‘Paul writes’, they are following the letter’s own words. Either way, the church has received the letter as Scripture.
Some of the earliest copies do not have the words “at Ephesus” in the first verse. So it may have been a circular letter, meant to be read in several churches across the region.

That is why the game is built the way it is. The walk shows the city of Paul’s years, about AD 52–55, but it is framed as a memory: the letter has just arrived, and an older member of the church is showing you the places its words bring to mind. No line of the letter turns up in the streets before it was written.

game.title: About this game
paragraphs: The streets, squares and great buildings follow what archaeologists have found, and we left out the famous ruins that were built after Paul’s time. Much is still guesswork. Every plaque has two parts, ‘What we know’ and ‘What’s imagined here’, and a ‘Location imagined’ badge marks places whose real spot nobody knows.

Every character is a fictional portrayal. That includes the people named in Acts, such as Priscilla, Aquila and Demetrius: their conversations are invented, built on what Acts says about them. Paul is given no invented words at all. In the riot scene, people speak only the words Acts gives them.

Scripture is quoted from the World English Bible, a modern translation in the public domain. Distances are shrunk so the city can be crossed in a few minutes. The real walk from the harbor to the Temple of Artemis would take far longer.

Historians disagree about some things, from how the theatre looked in the 50s to who wrote the letter. Where it can, the game says so instead of picking a side. If something puzzles you, that is a good question to bring to your group.
